title: All the Principles of Piety Subverted by Fanatics, Who Substitute Revelations for Scripture
sectionSummaries: 1. The temper and error of the Libertines, who take to themselves the name of spiritual, briefly described. Their refutation. 1. The Apostles and all true Christians have embraced the written Word. This confirmed by a passage in Isaiah; also by the example and words of Paul. 2. The Spirit of Christ seals the doctrine of the written Word on the minds of the godly.
2. Refutation continued. 3. The impositions of Satan cannot be detected without the aid of the written Word. First Objection. The Answer to it.
3. Second Objection from the words of Paul as to the letter and spirit . The Answer, with an explanation of Paul’s meaning. How the Spirit and the written Word are indissolubly connected.

paragraphs: Those who, rejecting Scripture, imagine that they have some peculiar way of penetrating to God, are to be deemed not so much under the influence of error as madness. For certain giddy men Lactantius: Cœlestes literas corruperunt, ut novam sibi doctrinam sine ulla radice ac stabilitate componerent. Vide Calvin in Instruct. adv. Libertinos, cap. 9 and 10.
For the Latin, “ac si elementarius esset,” the French has, “comme s’ils eussent étépetis enfans a l’A, B, C;”—as if they were little children at their A, B, C.

Hence it is easy to understand that we must give diligent heed both to the reading and hearing of Scripture, if we would obtain any benefit from the Spirit of God (just as Peter praises those who attentively study the doctrine of the prophets ( 2 Pet. 1:19 ), though it might have been thought to be superseded after the gospel light arose), and, on the contrary, that any spirit which passes by the wisdom of God’s Word, and suggests any other doctrine, is deservedly suspected of vanity and falsehood. Since Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, what authority can the Spirit have with us if he be not ascertained by an infallible mark? And assuredly he is pointed out to us by the Lord with sufficient clearness; but these miserable men err as if bent on their own destruction, while they seek the Spirit from themselves rather than from Him. But they say that it is insulting to subject the Spirit, to whom all things are to be subject, to the Scripture: as if it were disgraceful to the Holy Spirit to maintain a perfect resemblance throughout, and be in all respects without variation consistent with himself. True, if he were subjected to a human, an angelical, or to any foreign standard, it might be thought that he was rendered subordinate, or, if you will, brought into bondage, but so long as he is compared with himself, and considered in himself, how can it be said that he is thereby injured? I admit that he is brought to a test, but the very test by which it has pleased him that his majesty should be confirmed. It ought to be enough for us when once we hear his voice; but lest Satan should insinuate himself under his name, he wishes us to recognise him by the image which he has stamped on the Scriptures. The author of the Scriptures cannot vary, and change his likeness. Such as he there appeared at first, such he will perpetually remain. There is nothing contumelious to him in this, unless we are to think it would be honourable for him to degenerate, and revolt against himself.

Their cavil about our cleaving to the dead letter carries with it the punishment which they deserve for despising Scripture. It is clear that Paul is there arguing against false apostles ( 2 Cor. 3:6 ), who, by recommending the law without Christ, deprived the people of the benefit of the New Covenant, by which the Lord engages that he will write his law on the hearts of believers, and engrave it on their inward parts. The letter therefore is dead, and the law of the Lord kills its readers when it is dissevered from the grace of Christ, and only sounds in the ear without touching the heart. But if it is effectually impressed on the heart by the Spirit; if it exhibits Christ, it is the word of life converting the soul, and making wise the simple. Nay, in the very same passage, the apostle calls his own preaching the ministration of the Spirit ( 2 Cor. 3:8 ), intimating that the Holy Spirit so cleaves to his own truth, as he has expressed it in Scripture, that he then only exerts and puts forth his strength when the word is received with due honour and respect.

There is nothing repugnant here to what was lately said (chap. 7) that we have no great certainty of the word itself, until it be confirmed by the testimony of the Spirit. For the Lord has so knit together the certainty of his word and his Spirit, that our minds are duly imbued with reverence for the word when the Spirit shining upon it enables us there to behold the face of God; and, on the other hand, we embrace the Spirit with no danger of delusion when we recognise him in his image, that is, in his word. Thus, indeed, it is. God did not produce his word before men for the sake of sudden display, intending to abolish it the moment the Spirit should arrive; but he employed the same Spirit, by whose agency he had administered the word, to complete his work by the efficacious confirmation of the word. In this way Christ explained to the two disciples ( Luke 24:27 ), not that they were to reject the Scriptures and trust to their own wisdom, but that they were to understand the Scriptures. In like manner, when Paul says to the Thessalonians, “Quench not the Spirit,” he does not carry them aloft to empty speculation apart from the word; he immediately adds, “Despise not prophesying,” ( 1 Thess. 5:19, 20 ). By this, doubtless, he intimates that the light of the Spirit is quenched the moment prophesying fall into contempt. How is this answered by those swelling enthusiasts, in whose idea the only true illumination consists, in carelessly laying aside, and bidding adieu to the Word of God, while, with no less confidence than folly, they fasten upon any dreaming notion which may have casually sprung up in their minds? Surely a very different sobriety becomes the children of God. As they feel that without the Spirit of God they are utterly devoid of the light of truth, so they are not ignorant that the word is the instrument by which the illumination of the Spirit is dispensed. They know of no other Spirit than the one who dwelt and spake in the apostles—the Spirit by whose oracles they are daily invited to the hearing of the word.

application: Against the fanatics who set aside Scripture and chase private revelations, Calvin lays down a rule we dare not lose — the Spirit and the Word are knit together by God himself, never to be torn apart; the Spirit we are to follow is the one who spoke in the prophets and apostles, recognized by the very image he stamped on the page. Our generation has its own enthusiasts, no less confident: the impression that felt like a leading, the inner voice baptized as guidance, the conviction that maturity means moving beyond the old written Word into something fresher. Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, and a spirit that bypasses Scripture is rightly suspected of vanity. Try every prompting by the Word, for that is the test God himself appointed. The letter without the Spirit kills, but the Spirit never contradicts what he has written. Quench not the Spirit, Paul says — then in the same breath, despise not prophesying. Keep them married in your home, and you will not be led astray.

paragraphs: Those who reject Scripture and imagine that they have some special way of breaking through to God are to be judged as men driven not so much by error as by madness. For certain giddy men — Lactantius writes of such that they have corrupted the heavenly writings, so as to piece together for themselves a new doctrine with no root and no stability. See Calvin's Instruction against the Libertines, chapters 9 and 10.
Where the Latin reads "as if he were a raw beginner," the French has it this way: as if they were little children at their A, B, C.

From this it is easy to see that we must give careful attention both to the reading and to the hearing of Scripture, if we want to gain any benefit at all from the Spirit of God — just as Peter commends those who study the teaching of the prophets attentively (2 Peter 1:19), even though it might have been supposed that such study was set aside once the light of the gospel had dawned. And it is just as easy to see, on the other hand, that any spirit which bypasses the wisdom of God's Word and puts forward some other teaching is rightly suspected of emptiness and falsehood. Since Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, what authority can the Spirit have with us if he is not identified by some unfailing mark? And he is certainly pointed out to us by the Lord clearly enough; yet these wretched men go astray as though they were bent on their own ruin, since they look for the Spirit within themselves rather than from him. They object that it is an insult to place the Spirit, to whom all things ought to be subject, under the Scripture — as if it were a disgrace to the Holy Spirit to keep a perfect likeness throughout, and to be in every respect, without the slightest variation, consistent with himself. It is true that if he were made subject to a human standard, or an angelic one, or any standard outside himself, one might think he had been made subordinate, or, if you like, brought into bondage. But so long as he is compared with himself and considered in himself, how can anyone say that he is thereby wronged? I grant that he is brought to a test, but it is the very test by which he himself has been pleased to have his majesty confirmed. It ought to be enough for us once we have heard his voice; but so that Satan may not worm his way in under his name, he wants us to recognize him by the image he has stamped upon the Scriptures. The author of the Scriptures cannot shift and alter his likeness. As he first appeared there, so he will remain forever. There is nothing insulting to him in this, unless we are to suppose it would somehow be to his honor to degenerate and rebel against himself.

Their complaint that we cling to the dead letter carries within it the very punishment they deserve for despising Scripture. It is clear that Paul is there arguing against false apostles (2 Corinthians 3:6) who, by commending the law apart from Christ, robbed the people of the benefit of the New Covenant, in which the Lord pledges that he will write his law on the hearts of believers and engrave it on their inward parts. The letter, therefore, is dead, and the law of the Lord kills those who read it, when it is cut off from the grace of Christ and merely sounds in the ear without touching the heart. But if it is effectually pressed upon the heart by the Spirit, and if it sets Christ before us, then it is the word of life, converting the soul and making wise the simple. Indeed, in that very same passage the apostle calls his own preaching the ministration of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:8), indicating that the Holy Spirit clings so closely to his own truth, as he has set it down in Scripture, that he exerts and puts forth his strength only when the word is received with the honor and reverence that are due to it.

There is nothing here at odds with what was said a little earlier (chapter 7), that we have no firm certainty of the word itself until it is confirmed by the testimony of the Spirit. For the Lord has knit together the certainty of his word and of his Spirit so closely that our minds are rightly filled with reverence for the word when the Spirit, shining upon it, lets us behold the face of God there; and on the other hand, we embrace the Spirit with no danger of being deceived when we recognize him in his own image — that is, in his word. So indeed it stands. God did not set his word before men for the sake of a sudden display, meaning to do away with it the moment the Spirit should arrive; rather, he used that same Spirit, through whose working he had delivered the word, to finish his work by powerfully confirming that word. In this way Christ made it clear to the two disciples (Luke 24:27) not that they were to cast aside the Scriptures and lean on their own wisdom, but that they were to understand the Scriptures. In the same way, when Paul says to the Thessalonians, "Quench not the Spirit," he does not lift them up into empty speculation apart from the word; he immediately adds, "Despise not prophesying" (1 Thessalonians 5:19, 20). By this he surely means that the light of the Spirit is quenched the moment prophesying is held in contempt. What answer have those puffed-up enthusiasts to this — men in whose view the only true illumination lies in carelessly setting the Word of God aside and bidding it farewell, while with no less confidence than folly they seize upon whatever dreamy notion happens to have sprung up in their minds? Surely a very different sober-mindedness befits the children of God. Just as they are aware that without the Spirit of God they are utterly without the light of truth, so they are not ignorant that the word is the instrument by which the Spirit's illumination is given out. They know of no other Spirit than the one who dwelt and spoke in the apostles — the Spirit by whose own utterances they are daily invited to the hearing of the word.
